case.title: Rennowick has one pot for early releases: watch them or call victims
case.question: How should Rennowick spend its fixed £480,000 a year on the prisoners being released early into the town?
case.story: About 120 people serving short and medium sentences will come home to Rennowick over the next year under the early release scheme. The town's community safety group (made up) has one pot of £480,000 a year, set by the council and not able to grow. Quick check-ins by a supervisor in the first days cost about £300,000: six extra supervisors. Calling every victim back within 48 hours, with a named officer, costs about £250,000: five liaison staff. Both together cost £550,000. Some money could come from the youth service, which is also funded from this pot at £90,000, but cutting it would close two evening clubs.

in_the_news.headline: Hundreds more to walk free in latest phase of prison early release scheme
in_the_news.why: The story was from 10 November and still running: about 5,000 prisoners are being released early in stages. This made-up case imagines one town choosing how to spend a fixed pot on supervision and victims.

facts.text: About 5,000 prisoners in England and Wales are scheduled to be released early in stages over the next year, down from 6,000.
The third wave, about 650 prisoners released on 10 November 2026, covers sentences of between 882 and 1,163 days.
The government has announced £10 million for victim support alongside the early release scheme.

tests.text: Every person released into Rennowick is seen by a supervisor within 2 working days of release.
Every victim who asked is called back within 48 hours of the release date by a named officer.
Says how many staff are added and what they cost, so the total can be checked against £480,000.
Never spends more than the £480,000 pot or raises council tax to cover the gap.
Closes or cuts nothing in the youth service, including the two evening clubs.
Publishes every quarter how many check-ins were missed and how many victim calls went unanswered.

voices.text: I want to know someone has looked in on the man before he is back on my street. A week is too long.
If you have been hurt, the worst thing is a phone that never rings. Call the victim first.
Those two clubs keep the lads off the corner at night. Don't rob them to pay for this.
Tell us the count every quarter, including the bad news. Then we can judge you.

bench.angle: Supervise first: fast check-ins for everyone released
bench.title: Supervise first: six supervisors see everyone within 2 days
bench.answer: Rennowick's community safety group hires six supervisors (£300,000). Each person released is seen within 2 working days. It also hires three victim liaison staff (£150,000), who call victims who asked, within 48 hours, with a named officer. That is £450,000 in total, so £30,000 stays spare inside the £480,000 pot. Five liaison staff cost £250,000, which the pot can't buy. Three may not manage every call in busy weeks, and the spare £30,000 can pay for temporary cover. The youth service and both evening clubs stay untouched. There is no council tax rise. Every quarter the group publishes the check-ins missed and the victim calls unanswered, including the bad news. It has worked if both counts are near zero.

bench.title: Call every victim within 48 hours, with lighter supervision
bench.answer: Fund five victim liaison staff (£250,000) so every victim who asks gets a call within 48 hours of release from a named officer. Add two supervisors (£100,000, about £50,000 each). Keep the youth service at £90,000, so both evening clubs stay open. Total £440,000. The £40,000 left stays in reserve; the pot is never overspent and council tax does not rise. Two supervisors cannot see all 120 people in two days. They visit the highest-risk first. Others get a phone check-in. Every quarter, publish victim calls made on time and unanswered, and check-ins missed. Success is no victim call missed and a clear count of any missed check-ins.

bench.angle: Do both and pay by cutting the youth service
bench.title: Do both release checks and close the youth clubs to pay
bench.answer: Do both. Rennowick's community safety group hires six supervisors (£300,000) and five victim liaison staff (£250,000). That is 11 new staff and £550,000, which is £70,000 over the £480,000 pot. To close the gap, the council ends the £90,000 youth service. That closes the two evening clubs. The £20,000 left over covers training and phones. Nothing goes over £480,000 and council tax does not rise. Supervisors see every released person within 2 working days. A named officer calls each victim who asked within 48 hours. The group publishes every quarter the missed check-ins and the unanswered victim calls. It also reports any rise in night-time trouble where the clubs closed. The aim is zero missed check-ins and zero unanswered calls.

gate.verdict: No answer passes all six. A fails the 48-hour victim calls (three liaison staff can't cover them), B fails the 2-day supervision (two supervisors), and C meets both but closes the youth clubs, so every answer breaks one test or limit.

jury.question: The £480,000 pot cannot buy both fast supervisor check-ins and 48-hour victim call-backs. Which should come first?
options: Ask the council to raise the pot
jury.ruling: Supervisor check-ins come first, 5 votes to 4, with 3 wanting the council asked for more money.

reasons.text: I want someone to have looked in on him before he is back on my street.
The person who was hurt should hear from us first. Silence is cruel.
The pot is too small. Go back to the council and say so.

minister.text: Six supervisors see everyone released within 2 days and three liaison staff call victims. The trial tests whether three staff can make every 48-hour call-back, the one test it failed.
minister.statement: The money cannot buy both, and I will not pretend it can. Answer A passed five of six tests and stayed inside every limit: the pot, and the youth clubs. It failed one: three liaison staff cannot promise every victim a call in 48 hours. The jury said check-ins come first, 5 to 4, with 3 wanting more money. So we trial A for six months and count every missed call. Feeling safe and being safe are different. We will publish both numbers.
